# MAT11-1 — Foundations

## Course description

Every rigorous argument rests on the same three abilities: reasoning correctly, writing proofs properly, and manipulating expressions involving a variety of mathematical objects. This course aims to build all three.

Logic and set theory supply the vocabulary; proof methods then turn it into reusable templates. The course moves on to computation (via counting and standard sums and products), before deepening the study of functions and sequences. It closes with a study of the two central linear operators of analysis: differentiation and integration.

## Key topics

- Logic 
- Propositions, quantifiers ∀, ∃, ∃!, logical connectives ¬, ∧, ∨, ⇒, ⇔, truth tables 
- Vacuous truth, principle of explosion 
- Logical equivalence; law of excluded middle; involution of negation 
- De Morgan's laws 
- Distributivity of ∧ over ∨ and of ∨ over ∧ 
- Negation of a quantified statement
- Proof methods 
- Proof by contradiction 
- Proof by contrapositive 
- Proof by induction 
- Proof by exhaustive case distinction 
- Proof by analysis and synthesis
- Set theory 
- Sets, the empty set, singletons; N, Z, Q, R as given 
- Cardinality of a finite set; the power set P (X) and Card(P (X)) = 2n 
- Union, intersection, complement, set difference, Cartesian product 
- A = A, A ∩ A = ∅, A ∪ A = X 
- De Morgan's laws for sets; distributivity of ∪ over ∩
- Combinatorics 
- Factorial n!, convention 0! = 1, relation n! = n × (n − 1)! 
- Arrangements Akn 
- Binomial coefficient nk = n!k! (n − k)! and the symmetry nk = nn − k 
- Pascal's rule nk = n − 1k + n − 1k − 1 
- Pascal's triangle
- Sums and products 
- Notation ∑i ∈ I ai, ∏i ∈ I ai; convention for the empty sum and product 
- Linearity 
- Splitting a sum over a disjoint union of indices 
- Reindexing by translation 
- Telescoping 
- Binomial theorem 
- Geometric sum ∑nk = 0 qk = 1 − qn + 11 − q 
- Standard sums ∑ k, ∑ k2, ∑ k3
- Functions and infinite sets 
- Definition of a function through its graph; identity function; composition 
- Injectivity, surjectivity, bijectivity 
- Reciprocal of a bijection; composition of two bijections 
- Image f(A) and preimage f−1 (C) of a subset 
- Bijection theorem (continuous, strictly monotonic functions) 
- Equipotence, countable sets 
- Cantor's theorem (no surjection onto the power set) 
- Cantor–Bernstein theorem
- Sequences 
- Real sequences, explicit versus recursive definitions 
- ϵ–N definition of convergence; uniqueness of the limit 
- Every convergent sequence is bounded 
- Operations on limits (sum, scalar multiple, product, quotient) 
- The four indeterminate forms: ∞ − ∞, 0 × ∞, ∞ / ∞, 0 / 0 
- Arithmetico-geometric sequences, fixed point, closed form, convergence criterion |a| < 1 
- Squeeze theorem 
- Monotone sequence theorem: a monotone bounded sequence converges; an increasing unbounded sequence tends to +∞
- Differentiation 
- Continuity at a point; sequential characterization of continuity 
- Operations preserving continuity 
- Difference quotient, differentiability, tangent line 
- Differentiability implies continuity, not the converse 
- Points of non-differentiability: vertical tangent, angular point, oscillating quotient 
- Derivative of a sum, scalar multiple, product, quotient, composite 
- Local extremum at an interior point ⇒ critical point (converse false) 
- Sign of the derivative and monotonicity, via the mean value theorem 
- Second derivative; convexity and concavity; inflection points 
- Limit of a function at the bounds of its domain, including at infinity
- Integration 
- Primitive of a function on an interval 
- Existence on a segment; two primitives differ by a constant; linearity of primitives 
- Integral as an area, for a positive function 
- Extension to functions of arbitrary sign, algebraic area 
- Linearity of the integral 
- Chasles' relation 
- Exchanging the bounds 
- Fundamental theorem of calculus; ∫ba f = F(b) − F(a) 
- Integration by parts 
- Change of variable

## Learning outcomes

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. Construct truth tables, apply De Morgan's laws, and correctly negate statements involving quantifiers and logical connectives.
2. Write a correct proof by each of the five methods covered (contradiction, contrapositive, induction, exhaustion, analysis-synthesis), following the expected write-up structure.
3. Manipulate sets — membership, inclusion, power set, cardinality, union, intersection, complement, set difference, Cartesian product — and justify each step used.
4. Count permutations, arrangements, and combinations, and compute binomial coefficients using Pascal's rule and Pascal's triangle.
5. Manipulate sums and products in index notation — linearity, reindexing, telescoping — and apply the binomial theorem, geometric sums, and the standard sums ∑ k, ∑ k2, ∑ k3.
6. Determine whether a function is injective, surjective, or bijective, compute inverse functions, and work with the image and preimage of a set.
7. Determine whether two sets are equipotent, recognize countable sets, and apply Cantor's theorem and the Cantor–Bernstein theorem to compare infinite sets.
8. Determine whether a sequence converges, using the ϵ–N definition; show that a convergent sequence is bounded; and study an arithmetico-geometric sequence through its fixed point.
9. Compute derivatives using the differentiation rules, locate local extrema via Fermat's condition, and link the sign of the derivative to monotonicity.
10. Compute antiderivatives and definite integrals, using linearity, Chasles' relation, integration by parts and the change of variable formula, and interpret the integral as an area, connected to differentiation by the fundamental theorem of calculus.
11. Prove that for n ∈ N∗ and X a set with Card(X) = n, Card(P (X)) = 2n.
12. Prove that for n ∈ N∗ and k ∈ ⟦1, n⟧, nk = n − 1k + n − 1k − 1.
13. Prove that for n ∈ N∗ and q ∈ R ∖ {1}, ∑nk = 0 qk = 1 − qn + 11 − q.
14. Prove that for n ∈ N∗ and a, b ∈ R, (a + b)n = ∑nk = 0 nk ak bn − k.
15. Prove that for I an interval of R, f : I → R and a ∈ I interior to I, if f is differentiable at a and admits a local extremum at a, then f (a) = 0.
16. Prove that for I an interval of R, u, v : I → R of class C1 and a, b ∈ I, ∫ba u (t)  v(t)  d t = [u(t)  v(t)]ba − ∫ba u(t)  v (t)  d t.

### MCQ

No AI.
Tests maths readiness before taking Year 1. Pass (100/100) or fail (0/100). The score deciding pass or fail is computed as follows: every question carries the same weight, and within a question each correct option ticked earns an equal share of it while each incorrect option ticked cancels one such share, without ever going below 0. A student who does not pass sits a second BTS, of the same form and duration, whose result replaces the first.

### Written exam

Pen & Paper, no AI, closed book.
Early checkpoint: tests prerequisites and the grasp of the first concepts of the course. Informs teaching pace.

### Written exam

Pen & Paper, no AI, closed book.
Mid-course checkpoint: tests mastery of the material covered up to that point in the course.

### Written exam

Pen & Paper, no AI, closed book.
Tests problem-solving, proof construction, and applied mathematical reasoning under time constraint.
